1.Vide this judgment, I seek to dispose off the case of the prosecution filed against the accused Saurabh Dhingra S/o Sh. Ramesh Dhingra for having committed the offence punishable u/s 336 of Indian Penal Code, 1861 (hereinafter referred as "IPC") and 27/54/59 of the Arms Act, 1959 (hereinafter referred as "Arms Act").
2.Briefly stated, as per the case of the prosecution, on 28.01.2010 the accused Saurabh Dhingra had visited the Ashoka Hotel in his Maruti Swift car white colour car bearing no. DL CL 7142.
At about 4:10 AM, when the accused was exiting the Hotel in the said car, he had fired in the air from a country made pistol near the out gate of the hotel.
One empty cartridge was found near the spot.

After firing one round from the pistol, the accused fled away from the spot.

As per the prosecution,
the accused had fired from an unlicensed pistol and endangered the personal safety of the others.

3.After completing the formalities, the investigation was carried out by PS Chanakyapuri and a charge sheet was filed against the accused Saurabh Dhingra for the offence punishable u/s 336 IPC & 27/54/59 Arms Act.

Thereafter, cognisance was taken and charge was framed against the accused vide order dated 21.10.2014 for the offence punishable u/s 336 Digitally signed by ANIMESH ANIMESH KUMAR KUMAR Date:

HC Vikash Kumar, deposed as PW-11; and  HC Ashutosh, deposed as PW-12.
5.PW-1 Suresh Singh deposed that in the intervening night of 27/28 January, 2010, he was working as Security Supervisor at Ashoka Hotel.
On that day, he was performing his duty at control room from 9:30 PM to 7:30 PM.
At around 2 AM, he had received telephone call from a guard ANIMESH

He informed the duty officer, Ashoka Hotel regarding the incident.

In the cross-examination, he admitted that the date of the incident was intervening night of 27/28 January, 2010.
He did not remember as to whether the name of guard was Ramesh Chand who informed him regarding the incident.

He denied the suggestion that the name of guard was Ramesh Chand who informed him that one person had fired at the main out gate from vehicle bearing no. DL 1CL 7142 Swift white colour car, and thereafter, fled away from the spot with the said car.
He denied the suggestion that he was intentionally deposing falsely in order to save the accused as he was won over by the accused.

In the cross-examination, he stated that he was never called by any of the police officials at police station to enquire about the present case.

8.PW-2 Sh. A.P Singh deposed that in the intervening night of 27/28 January, 2010, he was posted as Manager, Security at Ashoka Hotel.

On that day at about 4 AM, his security supervisor Suresh Singh informed him that one person had fired in air at the main out gate of the Ashoka Hotel from Maruti swift car whose number he did not remember.
Thereafter he went there.
He asked Suresh Singh to check the CCTV footage in order to ascertain the registration number of Maruti swift car as well as manual register at the main out gate and main in gate.
After scrutiny, Suresh Singh confirmed the registration number of the white Maruti swift car.
Thereafter, he made a report in this regard to the Chief Security Officer Ex. PW-2/A.
He handed over empty cartridge with was handed over to him by Suresh Singh to the police in an envelope.

He correctly identified the empty cartridge which was produced in the Court in a white colour pullanda sealed with the seal of "SCT".

In the cross-examination, he interalia stated that he did not remember if he had stated in the incident report Ex. PW-2/A that he handed over empty cartridge to the police in envelope which was handed over to him by Digitally signed by ANIMESH ANIMESH KUMAR KUMAR

He also admitted that the CCTV camera was also installed in the parking of area of the hotel and it could be ascertained as to who who had parked and sat on the driver seat.

FINAL ARGUMENTS
24.During the final arguments, the Ld. APP submitted that the prosecution has successfully proved the guilt of the accused in the present case beyond reasonable doubts.
The eye witness PW-9 Ramesh Chand had correctly identified the accused in the Court.
The empty bullet cartridge was also recovered during the course of the investigation.
The vehicle used in the commission of the offence could be clearly seen in the CCTV footage.
Hence, the accused should be convicted in the present case.
25.Per contra, the Ld. Counsel for the accused, on the other hand, argued that the prosecution has failed to prove the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubts in the present case.
It was argued that the identity of the accused was doubtful in the present case in as much as the accused could not be identified properly by the eye witness PW-9.
No independent investigation was carried out by the investigating agency to establish the identity of the accused in the present case.

Also, the country made pistol from which the firing was allegedly done could not be recovered during the ANIMESH Date:
 KUMAR 2025.07.19 12  16:07:38  +0530 course of the investigation.
Thus, benefit of doubt needs to be extended to the accused.
26.I have heard the Ld. APP and Ld. defence counsel and have perused the case file.
27.Before, discussing the testimonies of PWs, it would be prudent to discuss the legal position involved in the present case.

LAW INVOLVED IN THE PRESENT CASE 28.Section 336 of the IPC provides for the offence of doing such acts which endanger human life or safety of others.

It reads as under:
"Whoever does any act so rashly or negligently as to endanger human life or the personal safety of others, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three months, or with fine which may extend to two hundred and fifty rupees, or with both"
29.Any
action that, due to its reckless or negligent nature, has the potential to cause harm or death to another person is an act endangering human life or safety of others.
This includes actions that may not necessarily result in injury but have a high risk of doing so.
30.Section 27 of the Arms Act provide punishment for using arms in contravention of provision enshrined u/s 5 & 7 of the Arms Act.
Section 5 ANIMESH KUMAR KUMAR

Date:
2025.07.19 16:07:45 +0530 regulates the licensing of arms and ammunition,
specifically for their manufacture, sale, transfer, and other related activities.
It stipulates that no one can engage in these activities without a valid license issued under the Act.

Section 7 prohibits the acquisition, possession, carrying, use,
manufacture, sale, transfer, conversion, repair, testing, or proofing of prohibited arms or ammunition without proper authorization from the Central Government.
ANALYSIS & FINDINGS 31.The accused Saurabh Dhingra has been charged for the offence punishable u/s 336 IPC and 27/54/59 of the Arms Act.

After perusing the materials available on record, I find that the prosecution has failed to prove the guilt of the accused Saurabh Dhingra in the present case beyond reasonable doubts for the reasons discussed in the subsequent paragraphs.

32.First and foremost, it should be noted that the prosecution failed to prove the most important fact that it was the accused Saurabh Dhingra who had fired in the air at the out gate of Ashoka Hotel at the time of the incident.

The eye witness of the present incident i.e. PW-9 Ramesh Chand could not properly identify the accused in his testimony before the Digitally signed by ANIMESH 14 ANIMESH KUMAR KUMAR Date:
2025.07.19 16:07:50 +0530 Court.
He had initially stated that he could not identify the accused.
However, when his attention was drawn towards the accused, he stated that "mujhe lag raha, yahi hai."
This would mean that the said witness was still not completely sure about the identity of the accused and some doubts were still in his mind.
In fact, in his cross-examination, he had stated that he had seen the accused for the first time in the Court.
It would mean that PW-9 did not see the accused at the spot at the time of the incident.

Thus, the testimony of PW-9 on the point of identity State vs Saurabh Dhingra on 18 July, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/73250334/
8 of the accused would not be of much help to the prosecution.
33.Further, the mother of the accused i.e. Anju Kumari who was the registered owner of the vehicle in question was never examined by the prosecution.

It should be noted that as per the prosecution,
the involvement of the accused in the present case was found in the investigation only when notice u/s 133 MV Act was served upon the registered owner who in her reply stated that it was her son i.e.
the accused who was driving his vehicle at the time of the incident.
Surprisingly, Anju Kumari was never examined by the prosecution.
Even her reply given to notice u/s 133 MV Act was not properly proved on record by the prosecution.

ANIMESH Date:
 KUMAR 2025.07.19  +0530 34.Moreover, the investigating agency did not collect any CCTV footage from the Ashoka Hotel which could show that the accused had indeed visited the said Hotel on the day of the incident.
It should be noted that the accused had allegedly fired in the air while exiting the Ashoka Hotel near his exit gate.
It would mean that the accused must have gone inside the Hotel either to have food or to meet some one or to stay.
The movement of the accused inside the hotel would have been easily covered in the CCTV footage.
However, surprisingly, the investigating agency did not make any effort to collect the said CCTV footages which would have been very crucial piece of evidence.
35.Also, even the CCTV footage of the parking area which was filed on record in a CD was never properly proved by the prosecution.
The custodian of the computer on which these CCTV footages were stored was not examined.
Even the relevant certificate u/s 65 B of the Indian Evidence Act was not filed on record.
36.Further, the investigating agency did also not make any effort to track the location of the mobile phone of the accused.

If the accused had gone to Ashoka Hotel and was using a mobile phone at that time, his presence at the hotel could also be proved by proving the location of his mobile phone at the time of the incident.
ANIMESH KUMAR  KUMAR

, in order to prove the culpability of the accused for the offence punishable u/s 27 of the Arms Act, it was imperative for the prosecution to prove that the accused had made firing from an unlicensed fire arm i.e. in contravention of section 5 of the Arms Act.

Thus, recovery of the said fire arm was of utmost importance in order to find out as to whether the accused had made firing from the said fire arm or not and also to find out as to whether the said fire arm was licensed or not.

The State vs Saurabh Dhingra on 18 July, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/73250334/
9
ballistic examination of the fire arm and blank cartridge recovered from the spot was required to be conducted.
However, the said fire arm / country made pistol could never be recovered during the course of the investigation.
Thus, the prosecution failed to prove the most important ingredient of the offence punishable u/s 27 Arms Act.

38.Therefore, in view of the above discussions and findings, I find that while there are grave suspicions against the accused for having committing the offences involved in the present case,
however, the prosecution has failed to prove his guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
Thus, benefit of doubts needs to be extended to the accused.
Thus, there are insufficient materials on record to convict the accused in the present case for the offence punishable u/s 336 IPC and 27/54/59 Arms Act.
39.Hence, the accused Saurabh Dhingra stands acquitted for the offence punishable u/s 336 IPC and 27/54/59 Arms Act.
